title: Report on Studying Abroad at the University of Adelaide
paragraphs: What does one go abroad to do? Various people say various things, and I think I decided to go to Australia half on impulse without really knowing. I told my teachers the commonplace reason of broadening my horizons, and joked to my friends that it was to escape clerkships in Japan, but in fact I did not even understand well what broadening one's horizons meant. What I simply think now that I have come back is that studying abroad was very effective in deflating an ego and self-esteem that had swollen big. To say something very embarrassing, before going I somehow thought of myself as "excellent." During clerkships, if you do the same studying as others faster than they do, you are praised with the word "excellent" for the time being. "A patient with a history of pelvic inflammatory disease complains of right upper quadrant pain, what do you suspect?" "Fitz-Hugh-Curtis!" I think I indulged in the empty word "excellent" obtained from question-and-answer exchanges like that, whose meaning I could not tell, while feeling a slight emptiness. Of course there are also such empty exchanges of knowledge overseas. At first I took part in such quiz battles, satisfying a certain pride while feeling dissatisfied.

After doing a clerkship at the Women's and Children's Hospital (WCH), a children's hospital in Adelaide, I did a clerkship at the Bunyarra Clinic in Whyalla, a clinic where three doctors work. The clerkship at the WCH was similar to polyclinic clerkships in Japan, and while receiving thorough guidance and classes, I was able to learn how to give presentations. The clerkship at the Bunyarra Clinic had a wonderful balance of laissez-faire and guidance, and the main daily routine was to interview patients by myself, form inferences about their illnesses, and then present to the doctor, and communicating with various patients was very stimulating for me, who had continued to study knowledge alone. What I felt in the process was my lack of ability. When a patient with depression cried, and when a patient suspected of myocardial infarction looked anxious, I did not know what to do. The "I'm sorry to hear that" that I thought I could just say meant nothing at all. Is this a problem of English ability? Seeing the doctor talk closely with patients and open their hearts, what I felt was that what I still lack is something like human ability rather than English ability. Also, the medical knowledge that I arrogantly thought I had to a reasonable degree was hardly useful in practice. The one month in Whyalla was long enough to make me keenly feel my lack of study and lack of human ability.

In this way, life in Whyalla taught me the difficulty and importance of working and of relating to people. Also, although this may sound paradoxical, I feel that at the same time I was able to realise the importance of knowledge. To give an example, when a patient in early pregnancy complained of diarrhea, the doctor in charge was about to prescribe a new quinolone, and in my poor English I stopped him, saying that I thought that would not do because it inhibits bone growth, and that was something I had gained from the knowledge battles I had thought were futile. I felt that the medical knowledge I had thought not very meaningful until then, and the things I had done until now, had a little meaning after all.

How one relates to people needs to change for each person, but most medical knowledge is probabilistically applicable to many people, so frankly it is cost-effective. Perhaps even such a simple thing becomes hard to see if one stays in one place all the time.

I felt that studying abroad resembled something, and it was the first month after entering university. I started living alone in Nagoya partly because I had grown tired of my parents' home, and what I felt afterward was the goodness of my parents' home and gratitude toward my parents. It is a very commonplace impression, but in the same way, through studying abroad I also came to understand a little the good points of Japanese education. The lectures during clerkships teach medicine and practice from the viewpoint of doctors, and above all they are in Japanese, so they are easy to understand. Although I did not really understand the point of watching surgeries that were too long all the time. Besides that, there are surely things one can understand by being apart, and there are cases where things I had thought unimportant look better after leaving, and the reverse. After finishing my study abroad, I still do not understand what it means for one's horizons to broaden, but perhaps it means looking from a little distance and accepting both the good and the bad.

Finally, I would like to thank very much the doctors of the International Collaboration Office, whom I troubled in various ways, the Frontier Association, which supported my study abroad from various directions, and the doctors at the University of Adelaide.
